name: Licorice root extract (glabridin)

lead: Licorice root extract is a plant-derived cosmetic ingredient whose glabridin component is promoted for brightening dark spots.

Its case rests on laboratory work: glabridin and related licorice compounds inhibited tyrosinase in cultured cells, and an extract fraction affected pigment and inflammation in guinea pig skin. The sources reviewed contain no human pigment trials.

paras: Glabridin inhibits tyrosinase, the enzyme that starts melanin synthesis, in cell models, and licorice compounds also show anti-inflammatory activity.
Topical risks are not quantified in the sources reviewed. Large oral licorice intake has documented adverse effects, and some constituents are estrogen-like in lab studies.

lead: Licorice root extract, from Glycyrrhiza glabra, is a botanical ingredient used in cosmetic brightening products. Its main skin-active component is glabridin, a hydrophobic isoflavane found in the root extract.[1][2]

Laboratory work has reported that glabridin inhibits tyrosinase activity in cultured mouse melanoma cells and had inhibitory effects on melanogenesis and inflammation in guinea pig skin, and other licorice constituents such as glabrene and isoliquiritigenin have also been reported as tyrosinase inhibitors.[3][4] Dermatology reviews list licorice-derived agents among non-hydroquinone lightening options.[5]
No human trial of licorice or glabridin for facial pigmentation appears among the sources reviewed for this entry; the registered trials of licorice extracts concern other conditions.
infobox: Glabridin is insoluble in water, soluble in organic solvents such as propylene glycol[2]

paras: Glabridin is a yellowish-brown powder of formula C20H20O4, classed as an isoflavane and natural phenol, and appears in the International Nomenclature of Cosmetic Ingredients.[2] A 1998 study described it as the main component of the hydrophobic fraction of licorice extract relevant to skin.[3]

In the 1998 laboratory study, glabridin inhibited tyrosinase in B16 murine melanoma cells at concentrations of roughly 0.1 to 1.0 microgram per milliliter without a detectable effect on their DNA synthesis, and a licorice fraction showed effects on melanogenesis and inflammation in guinea pig skin.[3] A 2003 paper reported glabrene and isoliquiritigenin as additional tyrosinase inhibitors from licorice roots.[4]
Licorice compounds have also been studied for anti-inflammatory activity, which is sometimes cited as relevant to post-inflammatory pigment.[6][7]

No studies found of licorice root extract or glabridin for skin lightening in people among the sources reviewed. Registered clinical trials of licorice extracts examine other conditions, such as hypertension, caries prevention, diabetic neuropathy, menopausal symptoms and stroke.[8][9][10] Evidence for the pigment use is therefore limited to laboratory and animal work.

Licorice taken by mouth in large amounts has been associated with documented adverse effects; a 2012 review of licorice abuse describes the problem as significant enough to warrant a warning message.[11] Some licorice constituents, including glabrene and isoliquiritigenin, show estrogen-like activity in laboratory studies.[12][13] These findings concern oral or experimental exposure; the sources reviewed do not quantify risks of topical cosmetic use.

Licorice extract is marketed as a botanical alternative within the wider market of non-hydroquinone lighteners, a category discussed in dermatology reviews against the background of debate over hydroquinone.[5]
